passage: Design tutor's note, Wednesday. Before opening any software, Tejas asked for a stack of blank cards and a marker. Naveen watched from the next bench. On each card Tejas drew a rough box and gave it a job: the problem, the method, the result, the next step. Twelve cards went on the table. Then came the cutting. "Does this one help tell the story?" Tejas asked, and four cards went into the bin, including a pretty diagram that led nowhere. The cards were moved around twice. Only after that did the laptop come out, and the slides took forty minutes. I did not give advice. I only noticed that the slides matched the cards exactly, and that Naveen asked to try the same method next week.

qa.q: How many cards went on the table, and how many were thrown away?
qa.a: Twelve cards went on the table, and four went into the bin.

qa.q: What was Tejas thinking when asking whether a card helped tell the story?
qa.a: Tejas felt determined and unsentimental, wanting every slide to serve the story and willing to throw away even a pretty diagram that led nowhere.

qa.q: What other approach could Tejas use if the story still feels unclear, and why?
qa.a: Tejas could tell the card sequence aloud to a listener, because gaps in the story show up quickly when someone listens.

qa.q: How might Naveen see the paper stage compared with opening the software straight away?
qa.a: Naveen saw a quicker and clearer route, so much so that Naveen asked to try the same method next week.

grounding: A student sketches each slide on paper as problem, method, result and next step, and cuts every slide that does not serve the story.

passage:
Sunday
Seminar talk on Thursday: fifteen minutes on our campus waste survey. Sarika, my project partner, wanted to open the slide software straight away and start picking templates. I said no, paper first.
We took an A3 sheet and drew twelve boxes. In each box we wrote what the slide must do: problem, method, result, or next step. Box 1: 'Hostels throw away 40 kg of food daily', with a sketch of a bin. Box 5: a quick bar chart. Box 11: what we want the college to change.
Then we asked of each box: does this help the story? Three boxes were just nice photos of us sorting rubbish. Out. One was a table of every bin's weight; it became one sentence on another slide.
Nine boxes left. Tonight we made the actual slides in forty minutes, because every decision was already on the paper.
– Imran

qa.q: How many boxes were left after cutting?
How does Imran seem to feel after making the slides in forty minutes?
qa.a: Imran seems pleased and relieved, since the paper plan made the slides quick and the story clear.

qa.q: What else could Imran and Sarika do before Thursday?
qa.a: Rehearse the nine slides aloud with a timer to check that the story fits fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How might Sarika see the paper step now?
qa.a: Sarika, who wanted to start on templates, sees that the paper plan cut the work and made the story clearer.

grounding: Shows students sketching every slide on paper as problem, method, result or next step, and cutting those that do not serve the story.
